summary:
Daniel Rosenwasser, Product Manager for TypeScript, presents TypeChat at the AI Engineer Summit 2023, an experimental npm library designed to bridge the gap between unstructured language model output and the structured data that traditional applications require. He frames the problem as a spectrum: chat interfaces like ChatGPT produce continuous flows of natural language, while conventional applications expect precise, structured data.

A naive approach—parsing natural language output by detecting patterns like numbered lines and colons—is fragile and unreliable. Merely asking the model for JSON improves things but remains insufficient: responses may contain unexpected properties or missing data, and describing complex schemas through examples leads to a combinatorial explosion of cases involving optional fields, nullable values, and union types.

TypeChat's central insight is that TypeScript type definitions serve a dual purpose: they guide the model toward producing correctly structured output, and they validate the results. The library leverages the TypeScript compiler under the hood for validation. When validation fails, the compiler's error messages are sent back to the model to attempt a repair, creating an iterative correction loop. This works because modern language models trained on both natural language and code can bridge these two worlds effectively.

Rosenwasser demonstrates TypeChat with a coffee shop example under 40 lines of code, showing how a JSON translator takes type definitions and user intent, producing well-typed output. A notable feature is the "unknown text" pattern: the schema includes a field for unrecognized input, allowing the application to report what it did not understand rather than silently failing. When a user orders "a purple gorilla named Bonsai," the model maps it to a bagel with butter but flags the unclear portion.

Beyond simple commands, TypeChat explores program generation for scripting applications. Rather than generating code in familiar languages where models tend to draw outside the lines, TypeChat uses a fake JSON-based language with refs to prior results—resembling SSA form—enabling type-safe chaining of operations. A fake TypeScript program is constructed in memory to validate that method calls and input types align. A calculator demo using a math schema, under 50 lines of code, demonstrates this program translator approach with an evaluate function acting as an instruction interpreter, effectively making a language model good at math.

TypeChat is being extended beyond TypeScript to other languages including Python, with promising early results using class methods and comments. A CSV manipulation example shows complex operations like filtering and joining. Rosenwasser closes by inviting attendees to try TypeChat, share feedback, and visit him at the Microsoft Booth to discuss bridging cutting-edge LLM capabilities to everyday engineers.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Problem Statement
sections.summary: Daniel introduces himself as TypeScript PM and presents TypeChat. The core problem: chat interfaces produce natural language while traditional apps need structured data. Parsing model output by detecting patterns like numbered lines and colons is fragile and unreliable.

sections.title: JSON Limitations and Types as Solution
sections.summary: Asking for JSON helps but is insufficient—validation is needed and example-based descriptions cause combinatorial explosion. TypeScript types solve both problems: they guide the model and validate results using the TypeScript compiler. Validation errors can be sent back to the model for repair.

sections.title: TypeChat Library and Coffee Shop Demo
sections.summary: TypeChat is on npm. The coffee shop demo takes natural language orders and produces structured output. The unknown text pattern lets schemas anticipate failure. The example is under 40 lines using a JSON translator with type definitions.

sections.title: Beyond Simple Commands: Code Generation Challenges
sections.summary: Exploring extension to scripting applications with chained commands and variables. Code generation raises sandboxing concerns—need to restrict loops and lambdas. Models draw outside the lines with familiar languages, motivating the type-driven approach.

sections.title: Program Generation with Fake Language and Math Demo
sections.summary: TypeChat generates a fake JSON-based language with refs to prior results (resembling SSA), constructs a fake TypeScript program in memory to validate method calls and type alignment. A math schema calculator demo under 50 lines uses a program translator with an evaluate function as an instruction interpreter, effectively making a language model good at math.

sections.title: Python Experiments and CSV Demo
sections.summary: TypeChat is being extended beyond TypeScript to Python with promising results using class methods and comments. A CSV example demonstrates column operations, filtering, and joining. Rosenwasser invites attendees to try TypeChat, share feedback, and visit him at the Microsoft Booth.

demonstrations: Coffee shop ordering example: "one latte with foam please" successfully parsed into structured JSON
Ambiguous order handling: "one latte and a medium purple gorilla named Bonsai" — model mapped Bonsai to a bagel but flagged unclear portion via unknown text
Coffee shop example shown to be under 40 lines of code
Calculator/math schema demo: "add 1 to 41 and then divide by 7" — program translator chains operations, under 50 lines of code
Python CSV example: reading CSV, filtering NA values, dropping rows, performing joins via program generation
limitations: Parsing natural language output is unreliable and fragile
Simply requesting JSON does not guarantee correct or complete data
Example-based prompting causes combinatorial explosion for complex schemas
Models tend to draw outside the lines with familiar languages like JavaScript or Python
Code generation requires sandboxing and safety constraints (no loops, no lambdas)
Models want to please users and may hallucinate plausible but incorrect mappings
Python support is a prototype, not prime time
Synchronous vs asynchronous API questions remain challenging for language models
